title: As much as you can
hook: be mindful of Allah as much as you are able (64:16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, qalb, and your line was he guides the heart through it. How did you meet your setback? Day six hundred thirty-one.

New Year's resolutions have a famous shelf life. Up at five every day. Gym seven days a week. Read a book a week. Never eat sugar again. By February, many of them are gone, and often the person feels worse than if they'd never started. The plan was too big to carry, so they carried none of it. Surah At-Taghabun, near its end, gives a command that sounds almost like a correction to that habit. It asks for everything, and then it adds four words.

Verse sixteen. Pickthall: "So keep your duty to Allah as best ye can". In Arabic: fattaqu llaha mastata'tum. Be mindful of God, as much as you are able. Mastata'tum: as far as you have the capacity. The verse goes on: listen, and obey, and spend; that's better for yourselves. Commentators set it beside a verse in Surah Al 'Imran that says: be mindful of God as he deserves to be. Some early scholars thought this verse eased the earlier one. Many others said the two explain each other: God deserves complete mindfulness, and what he asks of each person is that, within their real capacity. Surah Al-Baqarah says it as a principle. Pickthall: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." And the hadith makes it practical. Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet ﷺ saying: when I forbid you something, avoid it; when I command you something, do of it as much as you can. Another report in Bukhari says the deeds most loved by God are the ones done consistently, even if they're small. Put those together and you get a very different plan from a New Year's resolution. Not everything at once, then nothing. As much as you can, then keep going. The sick person prays sitting; if not sitting, lying down. The traveler shortens. The one who can't fast makes it up later or feeds the poor. Islamic law is full of these adjustments, and they all stand on this phrase. As much as you can is not an excuse for doing less. It's the measure that lets you keep doing it.
screen: `MASTATA'TUM: AS FAR AS YOU ARE ABLE.` · `NO SOUL TASKED BEYOND ITS SCOPE.` · `DO OF IT AS MUCH AS YOU CAN.` · `SMALL AND CONSTANT.`

segments.voice: The practice: do what you can, not more. Sit, and breathe. Think of one good intention you've let fall because it was too big: daily prayer, exercise, reading, calling home. Shrink it to a size you could truly do every day, even on a bad day. Five minutes. One page. One call a week. Picture doing that small version tomorrow, and the day after. Let your breath be easy, not forced, just as much as it is. The bell holds the time.
Istata'a: to have the capacity, the ability behind Surah At-Taghabun's command to be mindful of God as much as you are able. Today's word.
Your line: done consistently, even if small. Today, do the small version of your one good intention, once, and let that count. Day six hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Islamic law builds many concessions on this principle: the sick may pray sitting or lying down, travelers shorten prayers, and those unable to fast make up the days or feed the poor; many Muslims also favor small, steady devotions.

original.note: Arabic: so be mindful of God as much as you are able. istata'a means to be able, to have the capacity.

trapdoor: what you thought: an easy-going verse that lowers the bar.
what it means: full mindfulness, measured by real capacity, so it can be sustained.
what a scholar hears: 64:16 read with 3:102 (haqqa tuqatihi), some early scholars speaking of naskh, most of explanation; 2:286; Bukhari 7288 / Muslim 1337; Bukhari 6464 on constant deeds.
